profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This is a roughly 200 million dollar private enterprise data center in Sarpy County, Nebraska, in the La Vista and Papillion area south of Omaha, built by Travelers Insurance, part of The Travelers Companies, a Hartford, Connecticut headquartered property casualty insurer. The project was developed under the code name Project Oasis before Travelers was publicly identified as the company behind it, a common practice for large corporate data center projects negotiating incentives and land deals before revealing their identity. Local and trade press, including Data Center Dynamics, Insurance Journal, and the Omaha World-Herald, covered the facility opening around 2015 as part of a broader wave of large data center construction in Sarpy County during the 2010s. As an enterprise private data center for Travelers own internal insurance operations, including policy administration, claims processing, and disaster recovery, the facility is not marketed for third party colocation, and no specific critical IT megawattage figure beyond the roughly 200 million dollar construction cost was found published. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading.body:
The Travelers Insurance data center in Sarpy County, Nebraska, was built around 2015 as a private enterprise facility for internal insurance operations and does not market capacity to third parties. No critical IT megawatt figure has been published, though the construction cost of approximately 200 million dollars provides a rough scale; this sum typically corresponds to facilities in the range of tens of megawatts, but the operator has not disclosed the actual power draw. The facility sits in a state where 21 data center locations have been mapped but none publish their power capacity, making Nebraska opaque to any assessment of its role in AI infrastructure.

Because no megawatt figure is published for this site or any other facility in Nebraska, it cannot be ranked against peers by capacity or included in any calculation of the state's contribution to AI compute supply. The absence of published specifications across Nebraska's mapped facilities reflects the prevalence of private enterprise and legacy data centers that do not disclose their technical parameters to the public.

For a reader evaluating whether this campus matters to AI scaling, the relevant fact is that it is designed and operated for Travelers' own insurance claims and policy systems, not for AI workloads or general cloud compute. Without published power capacity or any indication of spare capacity for lease, it does not appear in the calculus of available compute for AI model training or inference.
